title: NL2Repo-Bench: Towards Long-Horizon Repository Generation Evaluation of Coding Agents
one_liner: Test coding agents on the hard part of software work: turning one requirements document and an empty folder into a complete installable library.
lead: Many coding benchmarks ask for a patch, a function, or a local repair. Those tasks matter, but they do not test whether an agent can hold a whole software project together over hundreds of steps. NL2Repo-Bench is built for that longer horizon. The agent gets one natural-language requirements document and an empty workspace, then must choose an architecture, create files, manage dependencies, and produce a Python library that installs and passes tests. The benchmark matters because it measures sustained project coherence rather than isolated code generation.

problem.h2: Why short coding tests miss the real difficulty
paras: A short coding task usually has a local target. Write this function. Repair this failing test. Fill this missing file. Success depends mostly on whether the agent can reason about the nearby code. A full repository build is different because early design choices determine whether much later files can fit together at all.

That longer horizon exposes failures that short tasks hide. An agent can write many locally plausible files and still fail the repository because the package layout is inconsistent, dependencies do not line up, the command-line entry points disagree with the modules, or the tests assume behavior that the earlier design never supported. NL2Repo-Bench is designed to make those long-range failures visible.

callout.html: Measure whether an agent can sustain design, implementation, and integration over a whole repository instead of only solving isolated code fragments.

panels.title: 1. Start from one requirements file
panels.caption: The agent gets only the project description and no starter code.

panels.title: 2. Pick an architecture
panels.caption: Early decisions create package structure, interfaces, and dependency boundaries.

panels.title: 3. Write many linked files
panels.caption: Each new file must agree with earlier design choices.

panels.title: 4. Integration cracks appear
panels.caption: One mismatch in names, imports, or assumptions can break the whole repository.

panels.title: 5. Run the full project
panels.caption: The benchmark scores whether the final repository actually works end to end.

steps.b: Give the agent one project description
steps.text: The input is a natural-language requirements document plus an empty workspace.
The agent must choose package structure, write source files, manage dependencies, and expose usable interfaces.
The repository is installed and tested instead of being judged only by surface similarity.
Open and closed models are evaluated under the same long-horizon build condition.
The benchmark records recurring breakdowns such as premature stopping, fragile cross-file links, and loss of overall plan.

paras: The paper changes the evaluation object from a local code edit to a whole repository produced from scratch and judged by execution.
object.object: a complete installable repository built from one requirements document

hidden.name: project-wide coherence
paras: The hard part of repository generation is not writing lines of code. The hard part is keeping every file consistent with one global design. Project-wide coherence means imports line up with the package layout, interfaces match the tests, and later modules honor assumptions made earlier.

NL2Repo-Bench makes this quantity visible because the repository is executed as a whole. A model can look productive while writing files, yet still have low coherence if the parts do not fit together. That is why average test pass rate stays low even for strong agents.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the repository-level links that must hold together for the project to pass execution.

reads.html: The benchmark is checking whether the whole project still makes sense after many steps, not whether a few files look reasonable on their own.
Long-horizon repository generation remains unsolved because agents lose global coherence across hundreds of interactions and produce fragile cross-file dependencies.

mechanism.h2: Why this benchmark exposes long-horizon weakness
paras: The benchmark works because it removes scaffolding. The agent is not given an existing repository whose structure can be copied and locally extended. It must choose the structure itself, then live with that choice across many later decisions. That setup makes planning errors expensive because a weak early design can force mismatches across the whole codebase.

Execution-based scoring is the second key piece. Surface plausibility is not enough. The repository must install, its modules must connect correctly, and its behavior must satisfy tests. This is what turns long-horizon coherence into something measurable, because execution fails the moment cross-file assumptions stop matching.

math.words: repository score = passed tests divided by all tests for the generated project

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a generated library is checked by 20 tests.
That 0.40 can still hide very uneven behavior: perhaps utility functions work, but package installation and cross-file interfaces fail.
The benchmark uses execution because a repository with RepoScore 0.40 is plainly incomplete even if many files look polished.

math.note: The paper also studies failure modes, but this score captures the main benchmark judgment: does the whole repository work?

charts.title: Short-horizon impression
charts.note: An agent can look strong on local tasks while still failing to finish a repository coherently.

charts.title: NL2Repo-Bench view
charts.note: The benchmark shows repository generation is still weak because coherence breaks across long chains of decisions.

items.html: The agent may stop after creating a plausible skeleton, but the repository is still unusable because required modules or wiring are missing.
A class name or interface can change in one file and not in another, which breaks execution because the project no longer agrees with itself.
A poor initial structure forces later patches to stack up awkwardly, because the repository keeps adapting around a bad foundation instead of following a clean plan.

A strong agent should keep an explicit project plan, update it as files are added, and re-check package structure, imports, and test assumptions after each major step so the repository stays coherent.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create five small library tasks from natural-language requirements only. For each task, ask an agent to build a complete Python package from an empty folder, including modules, package metadata, and tests. Run installation and test execution at the end.

Track both local progress and global success. Count files created, tests passed, and whether the final package installs cleanly. The demo should show that local file production does not guarantee a working repository because project-wide coherence is the real bottleneck.
demo.closing: A large coherence_gap would show that the agent can make many local steps look reasonable while still failing the full repository when everything is executed together.
